description_full: HEICO Corporation provides aerospace, defense, and electronic related products and services in the United States and internationally. Its Flight Support Group segment offers jet engine and aircraft component replacement parts; thermal insulation blankets and parts; renewable/reusable insulation systems; and specialty components and assemblies. This segment also distributes hydraulic, pneumatic, structural, interconnect, mechanical, and electro-mechanical components for the commercial, regional, and general aviation markets; and offers repair and overhaul services for jet engine and aircraft component parts, avionics, instruments, composites, and commercial aircraft surfaces, as well as for avionics and navigation systems, subcomponents, and other military aircraft instruments. The company's Electronic Technologies Group segment provides electro-optical infrared simulation and test equipment; electro-optical laser products; electro-optical, microwave, and other power equipment; electromagnetic and radio frequency (RF) interference shielding and suppression filters; power electronics; power conversion and interface products; interconnection devices; and underwater locator and emergency locator transmission beacons. This segment also offers traveling wave tube amplifiers and microwave power modules; memory products and specialty semiconductors; environment connectivity products and molded cable assemblies; RF and microwave products; communications and electronic intercept receivers and tuners; self-sealing auxiliary fuel systems; active antenna systems and airborne antennas; nuclear radiation detectors; power amplifiers; ceramic-to-metal feedthroughs and connectors; technical surveillance countermeasures equipment; RF receivers and sources; radiation assurance, embedded computing, and silicone solutions; test sockets and adapters; and electronic components and rotary joint assemblies. The company was incorporated in 1957 and is headquartered in Hollywood, Florida.

financial_summary: Heico Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $47.5B market cap on $4.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +27% over the past three years and +14% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 9% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $861M in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.35× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.8×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 23% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 138% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Significant goodwill (43% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.87, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $144.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 52% in the 2020 crash, 19% in the 2022 bear market and 60% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $143 (margin of safety -138%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 39%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $106 to $197 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 56.7 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 34.2 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 55.2 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 17% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $391 on average, 15% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.8%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.13).
It converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.35x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.7% of revenue on R&D.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($241.0M of cash against $2.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 7.8x.
Working capital ties up about 196 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
Goodwill makes up 43% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 26.6% over 3 years, 20.2% over 5 years and 14.2% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 17.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 12.2% on average.
own: Insiders own 22.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 81%.
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 2 sales over the past year.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 8.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 11,100 employees, each generates about $404K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 14.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $78K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.5M (14x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
